item.title: Angela Rayner urged to U-turn on rent controls – legal experts respond
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner is under increasing pressure to reconsider her stance on rent controls, with a group of MPs urging the government to address affordability issues in the private rental sector. A letter, spearheaded by Labour MP Chris Hinchliff, has garnered support from 26 MPs, including members of Labour, the Green Party, and former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn. The appeal calls for the introduction of rent controls to ease financial burdens on tenants. However, Rayner has previously dismissed the idea, citing concerns that such measures have not effectively reduced rents in other countries and highlighting the protections already offered by the Renters’ Rights Act.

The Debate Over Rent Controls

The government has firmly stated it has “no plans to introduce rent controls,” a position welcomed by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS). The think tank has warned that rent controls could have unintended consequences, including a potential reduction in housing supply and lower property prices. Whilst existing tenants might benefit from capped rent increases in the short term, the IFS argues that such policies could discourage landlords from maintaining their investments in the rental market.

IFS economists Matthew Oulton and Tom Wernham pointed to international evidence suggesting that rent controls often lead to a decline in both the availability and quality of rental properties. “Rent controls can reduce the supply of rental homes and negatively impact property sale prices,” they noted. Whilst a decrease in house prices might assist some renters in transitioning to homeownership, many would still face barriers due to insufficient income or savings for a deposit.

Potential Impact on the Rental Market

Kristine Ng, partner at Morr & Co, echoed the IFS’s concerns, emphasising that rent controls could deter investment in the private rented sector. “Whilst tenants may gain short-term security, the long-term risks to housing supply are significant,” she said. Ng highlighted that landlords may opt to sell their properties if returns become too restricted, potentially shrinking the rental market further. This, in turn, could exacerbate the existing housing shortage and place additional strain on the sector.

The IFS analysis suggests that a wave of landlords selling properties could lead to falling house prices, which might benefit some renters. However, the broader implications, such as reduced rental availability and potential declines in property maintenance standards, raise concerns about the sustainability of such a policy.

As the debate continues, homeowners and renters alike may wish to stay informed about potential changes to housing policies and their implications for the property market.

item.title: Burnham faces pressure for major property tax overhaul
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is under growing pressure to reform the UK’s property tax system, with campaigners and economists proposing a shift to a proportional property tax (PPT). The suggested overhaul would replace council tax and stamp duty with an annual levy based on current property values, potentially lowering bills for some homeowners whilst increasing contributions from owners of higher-value homes.

What Would a Proportional Property Tax Involve?

Under proposals championed by groups like Fairer Share and supported by some Labour figures, a PPT would introduce an annual charge of 0.48% of a property’s market value. Additional rates could apply to second homes (0.96%) and properties owned by foreign nationals. This system might particularly affect homeowners in London and the South East, where property values are typically higher, whilst potentially reducing costs for those in lower-value areas.

Economists suggest the reforms could redistribute tax burdens more equitably. Michael Jacobs, former adviser to Gordon Brown and editor of a Compass policy collection, notes that many households might see reduced bills under PPT. However, the proposals could prove politically challenging, as Burnham has indicated major reforms aren’t currently a priority despite his past support for fairer property taxation principles.

Broader Proposals for Tax Reform

The PPT forms part of wider suggestions for rebalancing the UK’s tax system. Professor Ben Ansell of Oxford University, writing for the IPPR, proposes aligning capital gains tax with income tax rates and extending National Insurance contributions to older workers. These measures aim to address generational inequalities, where younger workers currently bear a disproportionate tax burden compared to those who’ve benefited from rising property wealth.

Critics argue that sudden changes could destabilise the housing market, whilst supporters highlight potential benefits: simplified administration, reduced upfront costs for first-time buyers (through stamp duty abolition), and a system where tax contributions better reflect property values. The Fairer Share campaign estimates London alone might contribute an additional £7.5bn annually under their model.

With housing affordability remaining a key issue, these proposals are likely to fuel ongoing debates about fair taxation. Homeowners may wish to monitor developments, as any future changes could significantly affect household finances across different regions and property brackets.

item.title: Renters’ Rights Act drives more landlords into hands of letting agents
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

New research suggests private landlords are increasingly relying on letting agents to navigate the growing complexity of rental sector regulations. A survey by the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) reveals 66% of its members now use letting agents – the highest proportion recorded in at least two years. This shift comes as the sector prepares for further changes under the forthcoming Renters’ Rights Act.

Growing demand for professional management

The NRLA’s findings highlight how regulatory changes are reshaping landlord behaviour. With evolving tenancy laws and compliance requirements, many property owners appear to be opting for professional management services rather than handling tenancies themselves. The association notes this trend underlines the need for minimum education and training standards across the lettings industry.

However, tenant satisfaction data suggests room for improvement in agent-managed properties. Official figures show 73% of tenants with landlord-managed properties were satisfied with repairs, compared to just 59% in fully agent-managed homes. This disparity has prompted calls for better industry standards.

Calls for urgent regulatory reform

The NRLA is urging the government to accelerate plans for mandatory training requirements for letting agents, rather than waiting for a proposed consultation next year. Ben Beadle, NRLA chief executive, commented: “As the rental market becomes more complex, reliance on letting agents is only likely to grow further. Reforms to the agency sector should therefore go hand in hand with the wider changes to the rental market.”

While acknowledging that many agents provide excellent service, the association has expressed concerns about those lacking sufficient knowledge of legal responsibilities. Beadle added: “Minimum training standards would help ensure those working in the sector understand their responsibilities and can provide a consistently professional service.”

With two-thirds of rental properties now involving letting agents to some degree, these professional standards could become increasingly important for both landlords and tenants navigating the evolving private rental sector.

item.title: Property industry reacts to Zoopla House Price Index
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The latest Zoopla House Price Index indicates tentative signs of recovery in the UK property market, with buyer searches rising 7% annually despite ongoing affordability pressures. Industry experts caution that whilst activity is picking up after the summer lull, full market recovery remains constrained by higher mortgage costs and deposit requirements.

Autumn bounce expected as mortgage rates stabilise

Market analysts note that autumn typically brings increased housing activity, with this year's seasonal uplift potentially more pronounced than spring's modest recovery. Knight Frank's head of UK residential research observed that mortgage rates have stabilised, albeit approximately one percentage point higher than pre-2023 levels.

The relative absence of disruptive Budget speculation this summer has provided more stability for buyers considering their options. However, industry voices suggest that renewed political uncertainty or tax policy changes in the coming months could impact market momentum.

Affordability challenges persist for buyers

Whilst buyer interest shows signs of recovery, property professionals emphasise that affordability remains the primary market constraint. Compared to early 2023, households now face borrowing capacity reductions of around 9%, with first-time buyers particularly affected by the £18,200 higher deposits needed to maintain mortgage repayments at current rates.

Estate agents report growing buyer enquiries and search activity across all regions, though transaction volumes remain 6% below 2022 levels. The increased supply of available properties is providing buyers with more choice and helping moderate price growth, though regional variations mean market conditions differ significantly across the country.

  • Buyer searches up 7% year-on-year
  • Mortgage borrowing power down 9% from start of 2023
  • Sales agreed still 6% below last year's levels
  • First-time buyers needing £18,200 extra for deposits

Property professionals advise that local market knowledge will be crucial in the coming months, helping buyers understand realistic budgets and ensuring sellers price properties appropriately. Whilst the return of buyer demand is encouraging, experts agree that affordability constraints remain the key obstacle to a sustained market recovery.

item.title: House price growth shifts beyond the big cities
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research reveals a striking shift in UK house price growth, with commuter towns now outperforming their neighbouring city centres. The trend, identified across all major urban areas analysed, suggests a growing preference for suburban living amidst changing affordability pressures.

London leads the commuter belt surge

The capital has seen the most dramatic divergence between urban and suburban property values. While London itself recorded a 3.7% annual price decline, surrounding commuter towns witnessed a 0.9% increase - creating a 4.6 percentage point gap. This suggests many buyers are prioritising more affordable locations within reasonable travelling distance of central London workplaces.

Cardiff displayed the second-largest discrepancy, with 6.7% growth in commuter areas compared to 2.9% in the city centre. Nottingham and Birmingham followed similar patterns, where modest city price declines contrasted with steady growth in their suburbs. Even traditionally resilient northern cities weren't immune to this trend, with Glasgow's commuter belt growth doubling the city's rate at 5% versus 2.5%.

Regional variations in the urban-suburban divide

The research examined 12 major UK cities, finding consistent but varying degrees of commuter belt outperformance:

  • Manchester: 0.5% city growth vs 2.7% in commuter areas
  • Sheffield and Newcastle: 1.9-2 percentage point gaps favouring suburbs
  • Liverpool and Leeds: Minimal differences under 0.5 points
  • Bristol: Just 1 percentage point separating city and commuter growth

Verona Frankish, CEO of Yopa which conducted the research, noted: "Higher mortgage rates have significantly impacted buyer affordability in recent years. While conditions have improved somewhat, purchasers are making more calculated decisions about location versus budget."

The analysis suggests that whilst the suburban premium exists nationwide, its intensity varies considerably by region. Homeowners considering a move might find better value in commuter towns, particularly around high-pressure markets like London. However, those in northern cities may find the price differentials less compelling when weighing against commuting costs.

As mortgage rates remain elevated compared to historic lows, this urban-to-suburban shift could persist. Borrowers seeking maximum space for their budget may continue favouring locations that balance accessibility with relative affordability.

item.title: Overlooked housing scheme could unlock hundreds of stalled developments
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A rarely used affordable housing scheme could help revive hundreds of stalled property developments across England, according to new research from Savills. The Discounted Market Sale (DMS) model may offer a solution when developers struggle to find housing associations to purchase affordable homes required under Section 106 agreements.

Alternative route for stalled developments

Traditional Section 106 agreements typically require developers to provide affordable housing, with housing associations purchasing these properties. However, recent financial pressures have led many associations to reduce their buying activity. Research from the Home Builders Federation reveals approximately 8,500 consented affordable homes lacked buyers as of October 2025, with over 700 sites experiencing delays or stalling completely.

The situation particularly affects smaller housebuilders, who often rely on project-specific financing and may need to secure affordable housing buyers before progressing developments. Savills suggests greater flexibility to convert stalled Section 106 packages to DMS arrangements could help unlock these projects without requiring additional public funding.

How Discounted Market Sales work

DMS properties, which include First Homes, are sold at least 20% below market value, with this discount remaining permanently attached to the property for future buyers. Crucially, unlike traditional affordable housing models, DMS doesn't require housing association involvement, potentially making developments more viable.

Despite its potential, DMS currently represents less than 4% of affordable housing delivery, averaging just 1,760 completions annually over the past decade. Savills' research, supported by several industry bodies, indicates this model could play a much larger role in addressing housing shortages.

Significant potential buyer demand

Savills' analysis reveals substantial untapped demand for DMS properties. Their estimates suggest approximately 530,000 private renting families with children could afford a three-bedroom DMS home with a 30% discount and 5% deposit – representing 34% of such households. Even at a 20% discount, around 350,000 families would potentially qualify.

The research illustrates this using a hypothetical £300,000 property. At a 30% discount (£210,000), buyers would need a household income of around £49,000 with a 5% deposit. This compares to the £63,000 typically required for the full market price, potentially opening homeownership to many more families.

While challenges remain in implementing DMS more widely, the research highlights its potential to help unblock stalled developments and improve access to homeownership. As the housing market continues to face affordability pressures, alternative models like DMS may play an increasingly important role in meeting the UK's housing needs.

item.title: New initiative aims to help agents avoid costly mistakes
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Scottish letting agents and property professionals now have access to a new Continuing Professional Development (CPD) accredited training programme designed to enhance industry standards. Launched by SafeDeposits Scotland, the SDS Academy offers specialised courses focused on tenancy deposit protection, dispute resolution and inventory management.

Structured Training for Property Professionals

The SDS Academy provides two live courses delivered via Zoom alongside two on-demand modules developed in partnership with Inventory Hive. The Foundation course covers essential deposit protection legislation, compliance requirements and best practices throughout the tenancy lifecycle. Meanwhile, the Adjudication Workshop equips professionals with practical skills for early dispute resolution and negotiation of deposit deductions.

Participants who complete all four courses gain permission to display the SDS Academy Approved logo on their property inspection reports for 18 months. Industry specialists from SafeDeposits Scotland and the Tenancy Deposit Scheme (TDS) adjudication team will deliver the training, drawing upon real-world case studies from Scotland's private rented sector.

Focus on Inventory Best Practice

The complementary on-demand courses developed by Inventory Hive concentrate on improving the quality and consistency of property reports. Led by inventory trainer Tim Wakelin, the modules cover:

  • Pre-tenancy processes and check-in reports including terminology standards
  • Mid-term inspections and end-of-tenancy procedures
  • Legal considerations during property assessments
  • How adjudicators evaluate evidence during deposit disputes

The training specifically addresses common pain points such as fair wear and tear assessments and the principle of betterment - key factors in many deposit disagreements. By standardising reporting methods and improving documentation quality, the programme aims to reduce unnecessary disputes between landlords and tenants.

Industry Support for Professional Development

Richard Abbots, CEO of Inventory Hive, emphasised how the courses provide "advanced insight into how cases are assessed" while promoting early resolution of potential disputes. The programme's CPD accreditation ensures the training meets recognised professional standards, allowing agents to demonstrate their commitment to ongoing learning.

With the first Zoom sessions commencing in September 2026, property professionals in Scotland may wish to consider how this training could enhance their operational efficiency and dispute resolution capabilities. The scheme represents a significant investment in raising professional standards across Scotland's private rental sector.

item.title: EYE NEWS UPDATE: Land Registry shake-up opens up new data for estate agents
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

HM Land Registry has introduced new property identifiers to its monthly Price Paid Data, a move that could significantly improve accuracy for estate agents, lenders and property professionals. From 28th August, Unique Property Reference Numbers (UPRNs) and INSPIRE IDs will be available alongside transaction records for England and Wales, potentially transforming how property data is analysed and matched.

How the new identifiers improve property matching

The inclusion of UPRNs addresses a longstanding challenge in property data – accurately linking transactions to specific homes. Currently, systems often rely on addresses which can vary in format or change over time, leading to potential mismatches. With each property now having a consistent numerical identifier, estate agents and property portals may find it easier to:

  • Connect historic sale prices to the correct properties
  • Provide more accurate property histories to buyers
  • Reduce errors in market valuation reports
  • Combine Price Paid Data with other datasets more reliably

The INSPIRE IDs serve a different purpose by identifying land parcels spatially. This addition could prove particularly valuable for developers assessing site potential or investors analysing neighbourhood trends.

Potential benefits across the property sector

While estate agents stand to gain from more precise property matching, the changes could have wider implications across the housing market:

  • Lenders might benefit from improved accuracy during mortgage valuations
  • Property researchers could conduct more detailed street-level analysis
  • Local authorities may find planning decisions better informed
  • Homeowners might access more reliable sales history for their property

HM Land Registry has described this as part of a strategic plan to "unlock the value" of its data. The organisation plans to extend the use of these identifiers to other datasets later in the financial year, potentially creating further opportunities for innovation in property technology and market analysis.

For those involved in property transactions, these changes represent a quiet but significant evolution in how housing data is structured and utilised. As the system beds in, professionals across the sector may wish to explore how these new identifiers could enhance their own processes and services.

item.title: Letting agent accused of withholding deposits from more than 100 tenants
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

A West Midlands letting agency faces serious allegations after numerous tenants reported withheld deposits, while landlords claim unpaid rental income. Morgan, Payne & Knightly (MPK), operating across Birmingham, Telford and Wolverhampton, is under scrutiny following multiple county court judgments and Trading Standards reports involving hundreds of thousands of pounds.

Deposit protection failures under scrutiny

The case has highlighted critical concerns about deposit protection compliance in the private rental sector. Wolverhampton Trading Standards identified instances where MPK allegedly failed to place tenant deposits in government-approved schemes – a legal requirement in England and Wales. However, enforcement action reportedly wasn't pursued as the properties involved fell under different local authority jurisdictions.

Former employees from three MPK branches told investigators they never witnessed deposits being properly secured in regulated schemes. The agency's practices have also faced questions regarding tenant vetting processes, particularly after one landlord discovered their property being used as a cannabis farm without the agency's apparent knowledge.

Growing legal and regulatory pressure

Court records show multiple judgments against both the agency and its director, Amun Singh Judge, known professionally as Tony Singh. The unresolved cases span missing tenant deposits and alleged non-payment of landlord rents. Despite repeated attempts by journalists and authorities to contact Mr Singh for comment, no response has been forthcoming.

Local councils have adopted differing approaches to the allegations. While Telford & Wrekin Council found no evidence of trading standards breaches, the case raises questions about cross-border enforcement challenges in the lettings sector. Industry experts suggest renters and landlords affected by similar situations might wish to seek guidance from organisations like Shelter or the National Residential Landlords Association.

This case serves as a reminder of the importance of verifying that deposits are properly protected in approved schemes. Both tenants and landlords may benefit from regularly checking their deposit protection status and keeping thorough records of all rental transactions.

item.title: Agents hike fees as Renters’ Rights Act adds to landlord pressures
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The introduction of the Renters’ Rights Act has led to noticeable changes across the private rental sector, with letting agents increasing fees and landlords facing greater compliance burdens. Recent research suggests these reforms are reshaping landlord strategies, from tenant selection to property management.

Rising costs and compliance pressures

Nearly a quarter of landlords have reported higher letting agent fees since the Renters’ Rights Act came into force, according to a survey of 250 UK landlords. The legislation, which abolished Section 21 ‘no-fault’ evictions in May, has also increased administrative workloads – with half of landlords noting a heavier compliance burden.

Under the new rules, landlords must now use Section 8 notices when seeking possession, requiring specific legal grounds and extended waiting periods. For rent arrears cases, the notice period has doubled to four weeks before court proceedings can begin. Industry observers warn that existing court delays could further prolong the eviction process.

Changing landlord approaches

The reforms appear to be influencing how landlords approach tenant selection and retention. Two in five landlords have tightened their vetting procedures, while nearly 10% are focusing more on keeping good tenants to avoid turnover. These shifts come alongside growing concerns about tenancy fraud, which reportedly costs the sector £4.1bn annually.

Recent data suggests approximately 4% of rental applications show signs of potential fraud, prompting many landlords and agents to prioritise thorough referencing. With Section 21 no longer available as a safety net, making the right tenant choice initially has become crucial. As one industry expert noted, reversing a problematic tenancy has become significantly more challenging under the new legislation.

While the full impact of the Renters’ Rights Act continues to unfold, these early indicators suggest a rental market where due diligence and long-term tenant relationships may become increasingly important for landlords navigating the new regulatory landscape.

item.title: PM’s housing ambitions hit reality check
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The government’s latest funding allocation for affordable housing has raised questions about whether it can meet the prime minister’s ambitious social housing targets. Ministers have confirmed the first £10bn from the £39bn Affordable Homes Programme will deliver 70,000 properties outside London, with 60% earmarked for social rent and the remainder including shared ownership and sheltered accommodation.

Gap between ambition and delivery

Prime minister Andy Burnham had previously campaigned for the entire £39bn budget to focus solely on council housing, calling for funds to be “dedicated to council homes” during his Makerfield constituency campaign. The current plans represent a notable shift from this position, with only three local councils included among the 33 strategic partners receiving funding commitments.

London will receive a separate £6bn allocation at a later date, as the government works towards its decade-long target of 300,000 affordable homes. While the funding has been welcomed, housing experts suggest the current approach may fall short of delivering the “biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar period” that Burnham promised.

Industry reaction to housing plans

The New Economics Foundation has warned that with councils comprising just one tenth of delivery partners, the prime minister’s social housing ambitions face significant challenges. Molly Harris, senior researcher at the NEF, commented: “A secure, affordable home is the foundation for a good life. With over a million households on council waiting lists, today’s announcement should be a first step towards much larger-scale grant funding.”

Professional services firm Blick Rothenberg noted that while the £39bn fund is welcome, grants alone cannot build houses. Mark Cunningham, a partner at the firm, highlighted the practical challenges in translating funding into completed homes, suggesting the government may need to consider additional measures to accelerate delivery.

As the Affordable Homes Programme begins its rollout, housing advocates will be watching closely to see whether the government can bridge the gap between its funding commitments and the scale of housing need across the country.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Savills, one of the UK’s leading estate agencies, has bolstered its London residential sales teams with two senior appointments. Callum Hodgson has joined the firm’s Notting Hill office as a director, bringing over two decades of experience in the property sector. Specialising in north and central London, Hodgson will collaborate with director Dan Martin and work closely with Savills teams in Kensington, Mayfair, and Brook Green. His expertise is expected to strengthen the agency’s presence in these sought-after areas.

Expanding Expertise Across London

In addition to Hodgson’s appointment, Matt Smith has been named director of Savills’ Islington office. With more than 20 years of experience in the London property market, Smith will focus on family house sales in Barnsbury, Canonbury, and Highbury. Based at the Upper Street office, he will also work within Savills’ north and east London network, which includes Hackney, Victoria Park, Clerkenwell, Shoreditch, Canary Wharf, and Wapping. Both Hodgson and Smith will collaborate with other divisions of Savills, such as its new homes, Private Office, and Auctions teams, to provide comprehensive services to clients.

Leadership in the Guild of Property Professionals

Meanwhile, the Guild of Property Professionals has appointed Kate Taylor, director of Taylor & Co, to its National Advisory Council (NAC). The NAC plays a crucial role in advising The Guild on strategy and ensuring input from member agencies across the UK. Taylor brings over 25 years of property industry experience to the role, spanning residential sales, lettings, business management, marketing, and compliance. Since launching Taylor & Co in Abergavenny in 2019, she has expanded the agency’s services to include residential sales, lettings, land, and rural property across Monmouthshire and surrounding areas.

Before establishing her own agency, Taylor held senior roles at Newland Rennie and DJ&P Newland Rennie, progressing from residential sales manager to head of residential. Her responsibilities included managing multi-branch operations, overseeing teams of up to 30 staff, and leading business development projects. These initiatives included rebranding, website and database launches, staff development, and technology integration, including AI. Taylor’s extensive experience and leadership skills are expected to bring valuable insights to The Guild’s National Advisory Council.

What This Means for Homeowners

These appointments highlight the ongoing evolution of the UK property and mortgage sectors. For homeowners and prospective buyers, the expertise of seasoned professionals like Hodgson, Smith, and Taylor could translate into more tailored services and strategic advice. Whether navigating the competitive London property market or exploring rural and land opportunities, working with experienced professionals may help individuals make informed decisions.

As the property market continues to adapt to changing economic conditions, the insights and leadership provided by industry veterans could play a pivotal role in shaping its future.

item.title: Where are BTL landlords securing the strongest rental returns?
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Buy-to-let landlords across England are seeing varying rental yields, with northern cities and certain regional markets offering particularly strong returns, according to recent analysis. The Letting Partnership’s research reveals that the average nominal rental yield in England stands at 5.9%, based on an average property price of £293,262 and monthly rent of £1,446. However, some areas are delivering yields close to 7%, making them attractive options for property investors.

Top performers for rental yields

Newcastle upon Tyne leads the way with an estimated gross rental yield of 6.9%, underpinned by an average property price of £208,589 and monthly rent of £1,206. Close behind are Portsmouth and Manchester, both achieving yields of 6.5%. Southampton and Tower Hamlets in London follow with yields of 6.4%, while Bristol, Blackpool, and Nottingham each offer returns of 6.3%. Lincoln and Kingston upon Hull round out the list with yields of 6.2%.

These figures highlight the importance of location when it comes to buy-to-let investments. While property prices in these areas may be lower than in London and the South East, the rental yields they generate often outpace those in more expensive markets.

London’s contrasting picture

In contrast, London boroughs such as Westminster and Kensington and Chelsea demonstrate significantly lower yields, despite their high rental incomes. Westminster, for example, boasts an average monthly rent of £3,168 but delivers an estimated yield of just 4.5%. Similarly, Kensington and Chelsea’s average rent of £3,596 results in a yield of only 3.5%.

While these areas generate substantial annual rental incomes—£38,000 in Westminster and £43,000 in Kensington and Chelsea—their lower yields reflect the premium property prices in these boroughs. This stark difference underscores the trade-off between rental income and property value, which landlords might consider when choosing where to invest.

Regional opportunities for landlords

The research suggests that regional markets, particularly in the North of England, continue to offer some of the most favourable conditions for buy-to-let investors. These areas combine relatively affordable property prices with strong rental demand, resulting in higher yields. For landlords looking to maximise returns, exploring opportunities outside of London could prove beneficial.

Chris Mason, COO of The Letting Partnership, commented: “Yield is understandably front of mind for landlords, and, as the figures show, there are still parts of the country where investors can achieve very healthy returns.”

Ultimately, the choice of location depends on individual investment goals. While some landlords may prioritise high rental yields, others might focus on areas with long-term capital growth potential. Careful research and consideration of market trends could help investors make informed decisions that align with their financial objectives.

item.title: EA Masters: Vote now for your favourite property industry supplier
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK property industry’s most trusted suppliers are set to be honoured as voting opens for the 2026 Best EA Supplier Awards. This prestigious event, part of the EA Masters ceremony, will take place on 3 November at Evolution London. Estate agents nationwide can now rate their suppliers on a scale of one to 10, recognising those who have made a significant impact on their businesses.

Celebrating Excellence in the Property Industry

The Best EA Supplier Awards aim to shine a spotlight on the companies that support estate agents across the UK. Suppliers will be judged across three categories: Small, Medium, and Large, with Gold, Silver, and Bronze awards up for grabs in each. The Gold winners from these categories will then compete for the coveted title of Best EA Supplier of the Year. Last year’s winners, including Street Group, Dawsons Training, and Home Box Move, demonstrated the high standards of service that suppliers can achieve.

Heather Staff, co-founder of Street Group, expressed her gratitude for last year’s win, stating: “We measure our success by the success of our customers. Being recognised by the industry and voted for by agents, whilst seeing our clients win awards themselves, truly means the world to us.”

How the Awards Benefit the Industry

The awards not only celebrate outstanding suppliers but also provide a valuable benchmark for the property industry. Through the EA Masters ratings system, the top 10% of suppliers will receive an Excellent rating, while the top 5% will earn the Exceptional title. This independent feedback helps estate agents make informed decisions when choosing suppliers, fostering a culture of excellence and accountability.

Estate agents are encouraged to participate by casting their votes and leaving reviews for their suppliers. By doing so, they contribute to a transparent and collaborative industry environment. Voting is now open, and agents can submit their feedback here.

As the property industry continues to evolve, recognising the suppliers who drive its success remains crucial. The Best EA Supplier Awards offer a unique opportunity for estate agents to acknowledge the partners who help them thrive, whilst inspiring others to raise their standards. item.title: One month in, prime minister. Take the handbrake off, or watch Britain seize up
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

As the new Prime Minister settles into their role, the property market remains in a state of stagnation, awaiting decisive action to reignite its momentum. Housing transactions are a cornerstone of the UK economy, yet recent data suggests a concerning slowdown. With no immediate plans to reform stamp duty and ongoing uncertainty around potential tax changes, the market continues to face significant challenges. Addressing these issues could be crucial for stimulating growth and restoring confidence among buyers, sellers, and industry professionals alike.

The Current State of the Housing Market

Recent figures from Connells Group highlight a worrying trend in the property market. The time taken to progress from a sale agreement to the exchange of contracts has increased significantly, now averaging 104 days compared to just 73 days a decade ago. For leasehold properties, this figure rises to 155 days, further complicating the process. Alarmingly, one in three transactions collapses before reaching completion, leaving both buyers and sellers frustrated.

In April, 61% of deals took longer to reach exchange than it did to secure a buyer in the first place. This inefficiency places immense pressure on estate agents, conveyancers, and mortgage brokers, who are forced to navigate outdated and cumbersome processes. While the industry demonstrated its ability to accelerate transactions during the last stamp duty holiday, such urgency is absent in day-to-day operations. This raises questions about why, in an increasingly digital age, the property market remains burdened by antiquated procedures.

Challenges at Both Ends of the Market

The housing market faces two distinct yet interconnected challenges. In the second-hand property sector, supply is at a 12-year high, but many homes remain unsold due to a mismatch between sellers’ expectations and buyers’ willingness to pay. This pricing issue often leads to prolonged marketing periods and eventual price reductions. Estate agents play a pivotal role here, encouraging realistic valuations to facilitate quicker sales and keep the market moving.

Conversely, the new-build sector is grappling with a shortage of available properties. Fewer planning permissions and delays in construction have exacerbated the supply gap, leaving buyers with limited options. This imbalance underscores the need for a coordinated approach to address both ends of the market, ensuring that supply meets demand and transactions proceed more smoothly.

As the government considers its next steps, prioritising reforms to streamline the property transaction process and stimulate activity could prove vital. By tackling inefficiencies and fostering a more dynamic market, policymakers have the opportunity to unlock the housing sector’s potential as a driver of economic growth.

item.title: Estate agents feel the heat as property market cools
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK property market is experiencing a seasonal slowdown, with estate agents reporting weaker-than-usual activity this summer. According to a recent survey commissioned by GetAgent, 78% of estate agents anticipate a quieter period compared to typical summer levels. Whilst summer holidays traditionally see a dip in market activity, prolonged hot weather this year appears to have exacerbated the trend.

Summer Holidays and Hot Weather Impact Market Activity

The school holidays often lead to a reduction in both buyer and seller activity, and this year is no exception. Nearly two-thirds (64%) of estate agents noted that seller activity usually declines during this period, with 45% reporting a significant drop. Buyer demand follows a similar pattern, with 58% of agents stating they typically receive fewer enquiries during the summer break. Of these, 27% described the reduction as substantial.

However, this summer’s prolonged hot weather has added further pressure to the market. An overwhelming 91% of agents reported that the heat has reduced activity in their local markets, with 55% describing the impact as significant. Property viewings appear to have been most affected, cited by 53% of respondents, followed by buyer enquiries (28%) and seller enquiries (19%).

Estate Agents Face Increased Workloads Despite Slowdown

Whilst fewer buyers and sellers are entering the market, estate agents’ workloads have not necessarily decreased. In fact, 74% of agents said they remain as busy as usual or even busier, as they focus on progressing existing transactions towards exchange and completion. This period also coincides with staff holidays, which can add to the pressure. item.title: The property market: should we all go over Beachy Head or is the cavalry coming to our rescue?
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent developments in the UK property market have left many homeowners and potential buyers questioning what the future holds. With rising interest rates, increasing living costs, and a challenging economic landscape, some may feel uncertain about their next steps. However, understanding the current trends and exploring available options could help borrowers navigate these turbulent times.

Interest Rates and Mortgage Costs

One of the most pressing concerns for homeowners is the impact of rising interest rates on mortgage repayments. The Bank of England’s base rate has seen multiple increases over the past year, leading to higher borrowing costs for many. Those on variable-rate mortgages or nearing the end of fixed-term deals may find their monthly payments significantly higher. Borrowers might consider reviewing their mortgage arrangements, exploring remortgaging options, or seeking advice from a financial adviser to ensure they are on the most suitable deal.

The Housing Market Outlook

The UK housing market has experienced fluctuations in recent months, with some areas seeing price declines while others remain resilient. Factors such as inflation, energy costs, and broader economic uncertainty have contributed to this mixed picture. For those looking to buy, it could be worth researching local market conditions and being prepared for potential negotiation opportunities. Meanwhile, homeowners planning to sell may wish to ensure their property is competitively priced and presented to attract buyers in a slower market.

Government Support and Policy Changes

Government policies and initiatives can play a significant role in shaping the property market. Recent discussions around welfare reform, energy bill support, and housing supply have sparked debate about the long-term solutions needed to address affordability and accessibility. Whilst immediate relief measures, such as VAT reductions on energy bills, may offer some respite, broader structural changes could be required to stabilise the market. Borrowers and homeowners may wish to stay informed about policy developments that could impact their financial planning.

Navigating the current property market landscape may feel daunting, but staying informed and proactive can help homeowners and buyers make confident decisions. Whether it’s reviewing mortgage options, monitoring market trends, or keeping an eye on policy changes, taking steps to understand the situation could provide clarity during uncertain times.

item.title: Property industry leaders join forces to tackle transaction delays
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Property industry leaders have come together to form an advisory board aimed at tackling lengthy transaction times and reducing fall-through rates in the UK housing market. Spearheaded by BestAgent founder Charlie Lamdin, the board includes prominent figures from estate agency, conveyancing, and property technology sectors. Among the members are Yopa CEO Verona Frankish, Thomas Legal and Equilaw Group CEO Simon David, and DDRE Global founder Daniel Daggers. Rory Sutherland, president emeritus of Ogilvy Consulting, also joins as both an adviser and investor in BestAgent.

The initiative follows growing concerns over the efficiency and reliability of residential property transactions. According to the government’s Home Buying and Selling Reform Roadmap, published in June, the average transaction now takes approximately 120 days from offer acceptance to completion—significantly longer than in 2007. Additionally, around one in three transactions fails to reach completion, causing frustration for buyers and sellers alike.

Addressing the Challenges

The advisory board will support BestAgent in its mission to streamline the home-moving process, with a focus on halving transaction times and reducing fall-through rates. Lamdin highlights that delays often stem from misaligned incentives across the housing market, where estate agents compete for instructions, portals prioritise advertising, and professionals focus on isolated aspects of the process. By prioritising transparency and completed transactions, BestAgent aims to create a more cohesive and efficient system.

One of the company’s key strategies is its Find Your Agent service, which allows prospective sellers to invite local estate agents to pitch for their business. Sellers can watch short videos from participating agents before selecting individuals to visit their property for valuations and further discussions. Importantly, agents cannot pay for preferential positioning within the service, and only the agent ultimately chosen by the seller incurs a charge. This approach aims to level the playing field, giving independent agencies a fairer chance to compete against larger corporate businesses.

A Collaborative Approach

The board’s diverse expertise underscores the importance of collaboration in addressing systemic issues within the property market. Alongside industry leaders, the group includes Alex Groundwater, a former programme director at FT, Sony, Cisco, and Crown Estate; property acquisition specialist Jo Henry; Animos founder Andrew Tillard; and retired Charles Russell Speechly partner Nick Armstrong. Together, they will advise BestAgent as it refines its proposition and works towards its ambitious targets.

Lamdin emphasises that the UK is not lacking in property websites or estate agents but rather in completed moves. By fostering greater transparency and efficiency, BestAgent hopes to transform the home-moving experience for buyers and sellers across the country.

As the property market continues to evolve, initiatives like this could play a crucial role in reducing delays and improving outcomes for all parties involved. Homeowners looking to sell or buy may wish to explore services such as Find Your Agent to streamline their journey and make informed decisions.

item.title: Property investment firm acquires estate agency network with 104 franchisees
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Property investment specialist Sourced has expanded its operations into estate agency services following the acquisition of Open House Estate Agents. The deal adds 104 franchisees to Sourced's existing network of over 230 operators, while allowing Open House to maintain its current brand and business model.

Expanding property services

The acquisition brings together two Warrington-based property businesses with similar approaches to franchising. Both companies combine local operators with centralised technology and support systems. For Sourced, the move represents a strategic expansion from its core services in property investment, finance and lettings into residential sales and auctions.

Open House franchisees will gain access to Sourced's existing infrastructure, including an acquisition funding programme that could help them purchase letting agencies or property portfolios. The combined network now covers the full property transaction process - from investment and finance through to sales, lettings, auctions and management.

Shared business philosophy

Stephen Moss, head of Sourced, highlighted the alignment between the two companies: "What stood out was how closely Open House's approach matched our own. Both networks support ambitious local operators with the systems and opportunities of a national organisation."

Rather than making immediate changes, Sourced plans to focus on identifying synergies between the two networks. Moss emphasised: "We're not looking to alter what makes Open House successful - we want to build on it." The estate agency brings established sales and auctions expertise to the group, while Sourced can offer its wider property network and technology to Open House franchisees.

For property professionals considering franchise opportunities, the merger creates one of the UK's largest networks with over 330 operators nationwide. The combined resources could provide franchisees with enhanced support and growth potential across multiple property sectors.

item.title: Landlords in rent arrears hit record low
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research indicates that UK landlords are experiencing fewer rent arrears than ever before, alongside improving profitability across the private rental sector. The findings from Pegasus Insight suggest the buy-to-let market may be showing signs of stabilisation after recent economic challenges.

Record low arrears signal tenant resilience

The latest data reveals the proportion of landlords facing rental payment delays has fallen to its lowest level since records began. This improvement comes despite ongoing cost-of-living pressures, suggesting many tenants are prioritising rent payments even as household budgets remain tight.

Several factors may be contributing to this trend:

  • Strong employment figures maintaining tenant incomes
  • More landlords implementing thorough affordability checks
  • Increased use of rent payment technology reducing administrative delays

Rental yields remain healthy for investors

Alongside the reduction in arrears, the research highlights continued healthy yields across most UK regions. Rental demand continues to outstrip supply in many areas, allowing landlords to maintain competitive returns on their investments.

Property investors might note that regional variations persist, with northern cities typically offering higher gross yields than London and the South East. However, capital growth potential remains an important consideration when assessing overall returns.

While these positive indicators suggest some relief for landlords after a challenging period, market conditions remain complex. Those considering buy-to-let investments may wish to seek professional financial advice and carefully assess both local market conditions and their own circumstances before proceeding.
